parts.title: Activities for different needs
parts.instructions: Match each person to a suitable option. Some options are extra.
parts.passage:
A. Forest Steps
A Saturday walk for beginners. A guide shows you how to read a trail map and choose a safe route. We provide maps. The whole session is outdoors.

B. River Count
Help a researcher record water birds on Thursday afternoons. Bring binoculars if you have them. Volunteers should already be able to identify three common birds.

C. Quiet Corner
A short lunchtime session in the library. Learn a few ways to take a break from screens and prepare for an afternoon of study. No outdoor exercise.

D. New Routes
An evening climbing session with experienced instructors. You should already know basic climbing safety. Shoes and other equipment are included.

E. First Aid Basics
Learn what to do while waiting for help after a minor accident. The class takes place on Saturday, indoors. No experience is needed.

F. Garden Skills
A weekday morning group that grows food in small spaces. Learn to plant herbs and make simple containers out of old boxes.

parts.title: The week I changed one habit
parts.instructions: Read the text and choose one answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last month I decided to walk home after class three days a week. My friend Tom had been doing this for a year. He always arrived home in a good mood, even on days when he had a lot of homework. I thought walking was just a way of getting from one place to another, but he described it as the best part of his afternoon.

On my first day I planned to follow the shortest route. When I reached the main road, I realized I was still listening to messages and thinking about my homework. So I put my phone in my bag and took a quieter path beside the park. It added ten minutes to the walk, but I noticed things I would usually have missed. There were people playing chess, a market stall selling flowers and a bird that I couldn’t name.

After a week, I hadn’t finished any more homework than usual. What changed was how I felt when I sat down to do it. Instead of wanting to check my phone every few minutes, I could work for longer without stopping. I don’t walk every day, especially if it rains. But I have learned that protecting a little time between school and home makes the rest of the evening easier.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer decide to walk home?
options: Tom’s experience made the writer curious.
The writer needed to save money for flowers.
Tom asked the writer to train for a race.
The writer no longer had a phone.
questions.answer: Tom’s experience made the writer curious.
questions.explanation: Tom spoke positively about walking, so the writer decided to try it.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer leave the main road?
options: It was closed to people on foot.
Tom had taken a shortcut to the market.
The writer wanted a quieter walk away from messages.
The park route took less time.
questions.answer: The writer wanted a quieter walk away from messages.
questions.explanation: The writer put away the phone and took a quiet route beside the park.

questions.prompt: What did the writer notice after a week?
options: Homework took much less time.
It was easier to concentrate on homework.
The park route became shorter.
Tom had started walking every day.
questions.answer: It was easier to concentrate on homework.
questions.explanation: The volume of work stayed the same, but the writer could focus for longer.

questions.prompt: Which title best suits the text?
options: Why I stopped walking to school
A park that needs more visitors
A small break that helped me focus
How to finish every task before dinner
questions.answer: A small break that helped me focus
questions.explanation: The longer path became a useful break before afternoon work.

parts.title: A Saturday in the garden
parts.instructions: Four sentences are missing. Choose one sentence for each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
When I first joined the community garden, I expected to spend each Saturday planting vegetables. On my first day, a volunteer called Omar explained that some neighbors came mainly to get out of the house and talk to others. [1] From that day, I paid more attention to the people as well as the work.

One morning Omar showed me how to tell several herbs apart by their smell. I knew the names when he said them, but I couldn’t remember which plant was which. [2] The labels meant that I could practice on my own.

The week before our open day, a storm arrived suddenly. We were worried about the young plants in the most exposed part of the garden. [3] The next morning their leaves were still in good condition.

We put our herbs on a table for visitors on the open day. [4] Several people told us they would use them in their dinner that evening.

options: Fortunately, someone had already moved the seedlings under a shelter.
I decided to stop going to the garden every week.
That was the first time I thought of the garden as a place for more than plants.
We had grown enough to give each visitor a small bunch.
I asked him to write the names on labels so that I could check them later.
questions.answer: That was the first time I thought of the garden as a place for more than plants.
questions.explanation: The garden serves a social purpose as well as growing food.

parts.title: A new challenge
parts.instructions: Write one word in each numbered gap.
parts.passage:
Hi Max,
Have you ever (1) ____ sailing? I tried it last summer, and now I want to take another lesson. My friend Ada has been sailing (2) ____ two years. Tickets are cheaper online, so let’s book (3) ____ the website. If I were you, I (4) ____ bring a jacket even on a warm day. Would you like to come?
Dan

questions.explanation: Use a past participle after have you ever. Here, tried means taken part in the activity.
Use for with a period of time.
On the website means using the site to book. Equivalent one-word forms are accepted.
If I were you, I would gives advice about a hypothetical situation.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Read the questions. Listen twice and choose one answer for each question.
parts.transcript:
Narrator: Question one. You hear two friends talking after class.
Maya: You look tired, Alex. Were you up late doing your homework again?
Ben: I actually finished it before dinner. But I kept looking at my phone after I went to bed. I'm going to leave it downstairs tonight.
Maya: Good idea. It might be easier to sleep without it there.

Narrator: Question two. You hear two people deciding how to prepare a project.
Ben: Should we finish the slides first?
Maya: The slides can wait. If we don't agree on our main idea now, we'll have to do the work twice.
Ben: All right. Let's make a list of ideas and choose one.

Narrator: Question three. You hear two people discussing a walk.
Maya: Did you see any animals on your walk?
Ben: A lot of birds, but they kept flying away. The best part was reaching the top just as the clouds cleared. I could see all the way to the coast.
Maya: That sounds worth the long climb.

Narrator: Question four. You hear two friends discussing a new activity.
Ben: How was climbing?
Maya: My arms were tired afterward, but I found it much easier than I expected. The instructor explained things slowly, which helped. I'll try a harder route next time.

He used his phone in bed.
He was worried about class.

questions.explanation: He had finished the homework early. He says he kept looking at his phone.

parts.title: An interview about a challenge
parts.instructions: Read the questions. Listen twice and choose one answer for each question.
parts.transcript:
Narrator: You will hear an interview with a student who organized a screen-free evening.
Ben: What gave you the idea for a screen-free evening, Ella?
Maya: I saw a similar challenge online, but the idea only felt useful when my friends said we never finished a conversation without looking at our phones. We wanted an evening when we could really talk.
Ben: How did the first evening go?
Maya: I was worried that nobody would know what to do, so I brought a board game. In fact, we talked for the first hour and only opened the box later. We started too late, though, and some people had to catch the bus home before the game ended.
Ben: Will you run it again?
Maya: Yes, but next time we'll start earlier. I don't want everyone to give up their phones all the time. I just want them to notice when their phones get in the way.
